title: We Don't Need Another Hero? The Impact of "Heroes" on Software Development

edges.target: Yamashita et al. 80/20 Pareto hero-project definition
edges.ref: [39] Yamashita, McIntosh, Kamei, Hassan, Ubayashi. 2015. Revisiting the applicability of the pareto principle to core development teams in OSS. IWPSE.
edges.evidence: if the number of commits made by 20% of developers is more than 80% of the commits, they are classified as Hero Projects (thresholds selected based on the advice of Yamashita et al [39])

edges.target: Gautam et al. team-size bands (small/medium/large)
edges.ref: [14] Gautam, Vishwasrao, Servant. 2017. An empirical study of activity, popularity, size, testing, and stability in continuous integration. MSR.
edges.evidence: After applying the advice of Gautam et al. [14], we use 3 team sizes: Small teams: number of developers > 8 but less than 15

edges.target: Kalliamvakou et al. GitHub project filtering advice
edges.ref: [21] Kalliamvakou, Gousios, Blincoe, Singer, German, Damian. 2014. The promises and perils of mining github. MSR.
edges.evidence: We started off with 1,108 Public and 538 Enterprise Github projects. Following the advice of others [21] [5], we pruned as follows

edges.target: Bird et al. git-mining perils / filtering advice
edges.ref: [5] Bird, Rigby, Barr, Hamilton, German, Devanbu. 2009. The promises and perils of mining git. MSR.
edges.evidence: Following the advice of others [21] [5], we pruned as follows: Collaboration ... Commits ... Duration ... Issues ... Personal Purpose

edges.target: Munaiah et al. curating engineered GitHub projects
edges.ref: [29] Munaiah, Kroh, Cabrey, Nagappan. 2017. Curating GitHub for engineered software projects. Empirical Software Engineering.
edges.evidence: Studies done by [5, 21, 29] advice that researchers should filter out the projects which will not be suitable for analysis.

edges.target: GitHub Showcases project list
edges.ref: [16] Github. 2017. Github Showcases. https://github.com/showcases. [Online; accessed 13-October-2017].
edges.evidence: a selected set of projects are marked as showcases ... [16]. By selecting these Github projects we can ensure we are using an interesting and representative set of open source projects.

edges.target: GitHub API
edges.evidence: We used the Github API to extract necessary information from these projects and tested each criteria stated above.

edges.target: Scott-Knott ranking (Mittas & Angelis)
edges.ref: [25] Mittas and Angelis. 2013. Ranking and clustering software cost estimation models through a multiple comparisons algorithm. IEEE TSE 39(4).
edges.evidence: For the significance test, we use the Scott-Knott procedure recommended at TSE'13 [25] and ICSE'15 [15]. This technique recursively bi-clusters a sorted set of numbers.

edges.target: Scott-Knott ranking (Ghotra et al.)
edges.ref: [15] Ghotra, McIntosh, Hassan. 2015. Revisiting the impact of classification techniques on the performance of defect prediction models. ICSE, 789-800.
edges.evidence: we use the Scott-Knott procedure recommended at TSE'13 [25] and ICSE'15 [15]

edges.target: A12 effect size (Arcuri & Briand guide)
edges.ref: [1] Arcuri and Briand. 2011. A practical guide for using statistical tests to assess randomized algorithms in software engineering. ICSE, 1-10.
edges.evidence: our hypothesis test H was a conjunction of the A12 effect size test (endorsed by [1]) and nonparametric bootstrap sampling [13]

edges.target: Non-parametric bootstrap (Efron & Tibshirani)
edges.ref: [13] Efron and Tibshirani. 1994. An introduction to the bootstrap. Chapman and Hall, London.
edges.evidence: our Scott-Knott divided the data if both bootstrapping and an effect size test agreed that the division was statistically significant (90% confidence) and not a small effect (A12 >= 0.6)

edges.target: Cabot et al. issue label taxonomy (bug/enhancement tags)
edges.ref: [9] Cabot, Canovas Izquierdo, Cosentino, Rolandi. 2015. Exploring the use of labels to categorize issues in open-source software projects. SANER.
edges.evidence: To reduce the impact of this problem, we did take precautionary step to (e.g.,) include various tag identifiers from Cabot et al. [9].

edges.target: Kocaguneli et al. 'build effect' (Microsoft build engineers)
edges.ref: [22] Kocaguneli, Zimmermann, Bird, Nagappan, Menzies. 2013. Distributed development considered harmful?. ICSE, 882-890.
edges.evidence: Kocaguneli reported an extremely small number of build engineers (dozens, out of a total population of thousands of engineers). The heroes found in this study are far more frequent than that.

edges.target: Pinto et al. casual-contributor measurements (275 OSS projects)
edges.ref: [32] Pinto, Steinmacher, Gerosa. 2016. More common than you think: An in-depth study of casual contributors. SANER, 112-123.
edges.evidence: 77% and 78% projects are driven by hero or core developers in Public and Enterprise projects respectively. This trend was also observed by Pinto et al. [32].

edges.target: Brooks chief-programmer / 5-10x productivity conjecture
edges.ref: [8] Frederick P Brooks Jr. 1975. The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering, Anniversary Edition. Pearson Education India.
edges.evidence: our definition of hereos (80% of the work done by 20% of the developers) is consistent with the Brooks's conjecture that heroes are five times more productive than the other team members.

edges.target: Bier et al. 'communities of experts, not cowboy programmers' (anti-hero wisdom)
edges.ref: [4] Bier, Lovett, Seacord. 2011. An online learning approach to information systems security education. 15th CISSE.
edges.evidence: That is, contrary to established wisdom in the field [4], what we see here is most projects make extensive use of heroes.

edges.target: Ye & Kishida OSS developer-role taxonomy
edges.ref: [40] Ye and Kishida. 2003. Toward an understanding of the motivation Open Source Software developers. ICSE, 419-429.
edges.evidence: Following on from Ye and Martinez et al. [24, 40], we say that there are many developer roles within a Public or Enterprise software project: Project leaders ... Core members ...

edges.target: Martinez-Torres & Diaz-Fernandez OSS community roles
edges.ref: [24] Martinez-Torres and Diaz-Fernandez. 2014. Current issues and research trends on open-source software communities. Tech. Anal. & Strat. Mgmt.
edges.evidence: Such developers are sometimes called Hero/ Core/ lone contributors [24]. ... Following on from Ye and Martinez et al. [24, 40], we say that there are many developer roles

edges.target: Goeminne & Mens Pareto principle in OSS activity
edges.ref: [17] Goeminne and Mens. 2011. Evidence for the pareto principle in open source software activity. MDSM/SQM workshops, 74-82.
edges.evidence: In the literature [17, 35, 36, 39], it is usual to define a hero project as one where 80% of the contributions are made by 20% of the developers.

edges.target: Robles et al. core-team evolution (80/20 core definition)
edges.ref: [35] Robles, Gonzalez-Barahona, Herraiz. 2009. Evolution of the core team of developers in libre software projects. MSR, 167-170.
edges.evidence: Core developers are said to contribute roughly 80% of the code who are just about 20% of their project team size [17, 35, 36, 39].

edges.target: Martinez Torres et al. core team role analysis (80/20 core definition)
edges.ref: [36] Martinez Torres, Toral, Perales, Barrero. 2011. Analysis of the core team role in open source communities. CISIS, 109-114.
edges.evidence: Core developers are said to contribute roughly 80% of the code who are just about 20% of their project team size [17, 35, 36, 39].

edges.target: Jarczyk et al. GitHub quality metrics (issue resolution rate and time)
edges.ref: [20] Jarczyk, Gruszka, Jaroszewicz, Bukowski, Wierzbicki. 2014. Github projects. quality analysis of open-source software. SocInfo, 80-94.
edges.evidence: Lowering the issues/bugs/enhancements resolution times [2, 6, 18, 20, 26, 34]; Increasing the number of issues/bugs/enhancements being resolved [20].

edges.target: Bissyande et al. GitHub issue-tracker study (resolution-time metric)
edges.ref: [6] Bissyande, Lo, Jiang, Reveillere, Klein, Le Traon. 2013. Got issues? who cares about it? large scale investigation of github issue trackers. ISSRE
edges.evidence: Lowering the issues/bugs/enhancements resolution times [2, 6, 18, 20, 26, 34]

edges.target: Athanasiou et al. issue handling performance metric
edges.ref: [2] Athanasiou, Nugroho, Visser, Zaidman. 2014. Test code quality and its relation to issue handling performance. IEEE TSE 40(11), 1100-1125.
edges.evidence: Lowering the issues/bugs/enhancements resolution times [2, 6, 18, 20, 26, 34]

not_reuse_examples: [3] Bach 1995 'Enough about process: what we need are heroes' - background framing of the hero debate only; nothing adopted or tested.
[10, 12] Cosentino et al. / Dias et al. on GitHub social collaboration - cited only to motivate why collaboration might matter; no method, data or number reused.

[7, 19, 28, 38] Boehm / Hislop / Morcov / Wood-Harper - anti-hero anecdotes in related work; the paper argues against the consensus but never engages these specific claims, so only [4] is kept as the refuted target.
[37] Tsay et al. and [26] Mockus et al. - 'many eyes' / leader-does-most narrative used as post-hoc explanation for RQ1, not as an adopted method or quoted measurement.
notes: Empirical mining study (ICSE-SEIP'18) of 661 public + 171 IBM Enterprise GitHub projects; no baselines, no replication; single self-edge is Kocaguneli/Menzies 'build effect' used as a confound the authors argue away; Enterprise data is proprietary (industrial partner) with no citable source; GitHub API edge has no reference entry.
